items.title: The Breathing Gas
items.question: Which gas do green plants absorb from the air to make their food?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — carbon dioxide goes in, and oxygen comes out as the by-product.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: carbon dioxide. Plants pull it from the air and, with sunlight and water, turn it into sugar — releasing the oxygen we breathe as the leftover. Forests are net absorbers of exactly this gas.
items.lessonContent:
Photosynthesis runs on three inputs: light, water, and one airborne gas.
That gas has risen about fifty percent since industrialization began.
Plants return the favour as oxygen — the waste product we live on.
Oceans and forests split the absorbing work between them.
Share this: stand near one tree today and thank it for its half of your next breath.

items.title: The Golden Code
items.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Au, from aurum, the Latin word for gold.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Au. Chemical symbols descend from Latin names — aurum for gold, argentum for silver, ferrum for iron. Memorizing the Latin dozen unlocks most of the periodic table's odd-looking codes.
items.lessonContent:
Many element symbols are Latin fossils: Au from aurum, Ag from argentum, Fe from ferrum.
Latin was the shared language of early chemistry across Europe.
The dozen Latin-derived symbols are the only ones that look surprising.
Once you know aurum, Au stops being arbitrary and starts being history.
Share this: decode Na, K and Pb tonight using the same Latin trick.

items.title: The Heat Measurer
items.question: Which instrument measures temperature?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — a thermometer translates heat into a readable scale.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a thermometer. Whether mercury rising in glass or a digital probe changing resistance, the job is identical — convert molecular motion into a number. Galileo's air thermoscope was the great-grandparent of them all.
items.lessonContent:
Temperature is average molecular motion, and instruments convert that motion into numbers.
Old glass thermometers read expanding liquid; digital ones read changing resistance.
The Celsius scale pins 0 and 100 to water's freezing and boiling.
Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where motion itself stops.
Share this: guess the room's temperature before checking, and calibrate your inner scale.

items.title: The Frozen Form
items.question: What do you call water in its solid state?
items.correctExplanation: Right — ice: water's molecules locked into a crystal lattice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: ice. Cool liquid water below zero degrees and its molecules settle into a hexagonal crystal — the solid form of H2O. That lattice takes slightly more room than the liquid, which is the whole reason the cubes float.
items.lessonContent:
Freezing locks molecules into repeating crystal patterns instead of flowing freely.
Water's crystal is unusually spacious, so its solid floats on its liquid.
Snowflakes grow their six arms one water molecule at a time.
Glaciers are simply this crystal scaled to continents.
Share this: freeze water in a lidded bottle tonight and inspect the crystal bulge by morning.

items.title: The Leap Total
items.question: How many days are in a leap year?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — a leap year packs 366 days, one more than usual.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 366. Earth needs about 365 and a quarter days per orbit, and the leftover quarters accumulate — every four years we bank one extra day to resync the calendar. Without it, seasons would drift through the months.
items.lessonContent:
Earth's year is about 365.25 days, not a tidy integer — calendars must absorb the fraction.
Banking one day every four years keeps seasons pinned to their months.
Century years skip the leap unless divisible by 400 — 2000 qualified, 1900 did not.
The drift it prevents would otherwise move summer through winter over centuries.
Share this: ask someone born on February 29th how they count birthdays.

items.title: The Closest Orbit
items.question: Which planet orbits closest to the Sun?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Mercury, sprinting around the Sun in just 88 days.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mercury. It hugs the Sun closer than any sibling world, racing through its year in 88 Earth days. Its sun-baked dayside and frozen nightside make it the solar system's most extreme commuter.
items.lessonContent:
Mercury orbits nearest the Sun, completing a year in 88 Earth days.
Proximity means extremes: scorching dayside, frozen nightside, almost no air to even things out.
Its oddly precessing orbit once puzzled Newton — only relativity explained the wobble.
A year there is shorter than a single one of its solar days.
Share this: look up Mercury's next evening appearance and catch the swift planet yourself.

items.title: The Body Pump
items.question: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the heart: a fist-sized muscle beating about 100,000 times a day.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the heart. This double pump pushes blood to the lungs and body in one loop, never resting between beats. It moves roughly 7,500 litres daily through 100,000 kilometres of vessels.
items.lessonContent:
The heart is a double pump: right side to the lungs, left side to everything else.
It beats around 100,000 times a day without maintenance downtime.
Its vessels laid end to end would circle the planet twice.
Exercise remodels it like any muscle — athletes grow measurably larger ones.
Share this: find your pulse tonight and count the beats in a full resting minute.

items.title: The Air Majority
items.question: Which gas makes up most of the air you breathe?
items.correctExplanation: Right — nitrogen: nearly four-fifths of every breath, inert and mostly along for the ride.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nitrogen. About 78% of air is nitrogen, versus 21% oxygen — the famous one-fifth we actually use. Nitrogen's talent is stability: it dilutes oxygen to breathable strength without reacting with much.
items.lessonContent:
Air is mostly nitrogen — 78% inert background gas, with oxygen second at 21%.
Nitrogen's laziness is a feature: it dilutes oxygen to safe, breathable strength.
Lightning fixes a little of it into soil food each storm.
Divers breathe doctored mixes precisely to dodge nitrogen's deep-water effects.
Share this: tell someone tonight that each breath is mostly one gas they never use.

items.title: The Hardest Stone
items.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance known?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — diamond: carbon locked in the tightest crystal lattice nature builds.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: diamond. Every carbon atom grips four neighbours in a perfect tetrahedron, and that geometry defeats every other natural material. Only another one of its kind can cut it — which is why industrial drills wear it.
items.lessonContent:
Hardness is resistance to scratching, and carbon's tetrahedral lattice wins outright.
Graphite is the same atoms rearranged loosely — pencil lead versus jewel.
Structure, not just chemistry, decides a material's character.
Labs now grow gem-grade crystals that jewellers accept as genuine.
Share this: press a pencil tip and remember it shares atoms with the hardest thing known.

items.title: The Positive Core
items.question: What positively charged particles sit in an atom's nucleus?
items.correctExplanation: Right — protons: the positive residents of the nucleus, and their count defines each element.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: protons. The number of protons in the nucleus is an element's atomic number — its entire identity. Neutrons add weight without charge; electrons, far lighter, orbit the whole assembly.
items.lessonContent:
Protons carry the atom's positive charge and define its element — change the count, change the substance.
Rutherford found the nucleus by firing particles at gold foil and watching them bounce.
Neutrons pad the mass; electrons, two thousand times lighter, do the chemistry.
Stars forge heavier nuclei by fusing lighter ones under crushing heat.
Share this: recite hydrogen, helium, lithium tonight — the first three proton counts.

items.title: The Honey Source
items.question: What sweet substance do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — nectar: the sugary bribe flowers offer in exchange for pollination.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nectar. Bees haul this sugary liquid home, fan off its water, and seal the result as honey. Flowers evolved the bribe; bees evolved the collection service — pollination is the trade both sides signed.
items.lessonContent:
Nectar is a flower's payment to pollinators — sugar water offered for delivery services.
Bees evaporate most of its water and add enzymes to finish the honey.
Flowers advertise with colour and scent tuned to their couriers' senses.
The whole exchange is a contract written in chemistry.
Share this: watch one bee work a flowerbed and read the trade happening.

items.title: The Red World
items.question: Which planet is nicknamed the Red Planet?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Mars, stained red by iron oxide dust across its deserts.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mars. Its soil is rich in rusted iron, which dyes the whole world salmon-pink through telescopes. Ancient cultures named it for war on that colour alone, long before rovers confirmed the chemistry.
items.lessonContent:
Mars is red because it is rusty: iron oxide dust coats the surface and tints its sky.
Iron-rich rock plus ancient water chemistry plus wind equals a planet-wide patina.
The colour earned it war-god names across unrelated cultures.
Its sunsets reverse ours — blue halos around a dimmer Sun.
Share this: find a rusted bolt tonight and announce you are holding a piece of Mars's wardrobe.

items.title: The Vast Ocean
items.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the Pacific: wider than the Moon's diameter and deeper than Everest is tall.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Pacific. It sprawls across a third of Earth's surface — every continent could fit inside it with room to spare. Magellan named it for its calm, though typhoons would like a word.
items.lessonContent:
The Pacific covers a third of Earth's surface — wider than the Moon is round.
Its trenches plunge past eleven kilometres, deeper than Everest stands tall.
The 'Ring of Fire' rims it with the planet's most violent geology.
Magellan's crew crossed it in 99 days without resupply — and named it peaceful.
Share this: spin a globe tonight and note how much of it is one blue expanse.

items.title: Downward Always
items.question: What invisible force pulls falling objects toward the ground?
items.correctExplanation: Right — gravity: Earth's mass tugging everything toward its centre.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: gravity. Every mass attracts every other mass, and Earth's bulk wins every local contest — pulling apples, tides and satellites along their paths. Einstein later reframed it as spacetime itself curving around mass.
items.lessonContent:
Gravity is mutual attraction between masses — Earth wins every nearby contest by sheer bulk.
It holds the Moon in orbit and the coffee in your cup.
Einstein's upgrade: mass dents spacetime, and falling is rolling downhill in four dimensions.
Weighing less on the Moon is the same force with a smaller planet behind it.
Share this: drop two different objects tonight and watch gravity refuse to discriminate.

items.title: The Ringed Giant
items.question: Which planet is famous for its spectacular system of rings?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Saturn, girdled by rings of ice and rock hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Saturn. Its rings are billions of chunks of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized boulders — spanning a vast disc yet in places only ten metres thick. Other giants wear faint rings too; none wear them like this.
items.lessonContent:
Saturn's rings are ice and rock in billions of pieces, from dust to boulders.
The span is planetary, the thickness in places just ten metres — a sheet of debris of absurd proportions.
Shepherd moons braid and gap the rings into structure.
The rings are likely young, and possibly temporary on cosmic timescales.
Share this: describe the rings tonight as 'a snowstorm a hundred thousand kilometres wide, thinner than a house'.

items.title: The Solar Center
items.question: What sits at the centre of our solar system, holding the planets in orbit?
items.correctExplanation: Right — the Sun: 99.8% of the system's mass, and gravity does the rest.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the Sun. It holds 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system, so its gravity dictates every orbit. Placing it at the centre took humanity until Copernicus — the sky looks geocentric until the mathematics is done.
items.lessonContent:
The Sun owns 99.8% of the solar system's mass — the planets are crumbs by comparison.
Its gravity choreographs every orbit, from Mercury's sprint to Neptune's crawl.
Moving Earth from the centre took Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo combined.
A million Earths would fit inside it with room to spare.
Share this: hold a peppercorn at arm's length tonight and call it the scale of us to it.

items.title: The Breath Gas
items.question: Which gas do humans need to breathe in to survive?
items.correctExplanation: Right — oxygen: the electron acceptor your cells use to unlock food's energy.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: oxygen. It is the terminal partner in your energy chemistry — without it, the mitochondrial assembly line stalls within minutes. Brain cells die fastest, which is why breathing outranks every other priority.
items.lessonContent:
Oxygen is the acceptor that lets cells unlock food's stored energy — the fire that burns your fuel.
The brain consumes a fifth of it and tolerates minutes without it at most.
Plants exhale it as photosynthesis's waste — it is literally their exhaust.
Too much of it is also toxic; medicine doses it carefully.
Share this: take one deliberate slow breath and name the molecule doing the work.

items.title: The Common Name
items.question: What is H2O commonly called?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — water: two hydrogens and one oxygen wearing the plainest name in science.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: water. The most common compound on Earth's surface hides behind a one-syllable everyday word instead of its formula. Chemists named thousands of substances systematically, then left the most important one with its childhood nickname.
items.lessonContent:
Water's formula hides in plain sight: H2O, two hydrogens per oxygen.
Systematic naming would call it dihydrogen monoxide — nobody does.
The everyday name survived because the substance predates chemistry itself.
Ice, steam and liquid are one compound in three costumes.
Share this: say 'dihydrogen monoxide' with a straight face tonight and watch the room.

items.title: The Faster Messenger
items.question: Which travels faster: light or sound?
items.correctExplanation: Right — light outruns sound by roughly a million to one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: light. At 300,000 kilometres per second against sound's mere 343 metres, the race is not close — thunder always arrives as old news. The lightning-then-thunder delay is this gap made visible.
items.lessonContent:
Light beats sound by about a million to one — the gap behind every flash-then-rumble.
Count seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by three: kilometres to the storm.
Concert-goers far from the stage hear the delayed truth of it.
The ratio is why the sky can be silent while still flashing.
Share this: time one storm's gap tonight and announce the storm's distance.

items.title: The Web Spinners
items.question: How many legs does a spider have?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — eight: the arachnid signature, two more than any insect.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: eight. Spiders are arachnids, not insects, and the leg count is the quickest field mark — six means insect, eight means spider. Harvestmen and ticks keep the same family number.
items.lessonContent:
Eight legs mark the arachnids: spiders, scorpions, ticks and harvestmen.
Insects stop at six — the two extra legs are the field test.
Leg one on each side often works as a feeler, tasting and touching.
Spiders taste with their feet, which reframes every web they walk.
Share this: count the next spider's legs before deciding what it is.

items.title: Martian Companions
items.question: How many moons does Mars have?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two lumpy captured asteroids: Phobos and Deimos, fear and panic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: two. Phobos and Deimos are captured asteroids, too small to have rounded themselves — potatoes in orbit. Phobos is slowly spiralling inward and will one day shatter into a ring around Mars.
items.lessonContent:
Mars keeps two captured asteroids as moons — lumpy, cratered potatoes.
Phobos orbits so fast it rises twice per Martian day.
It is also doomed: spiralling inward, it will one day shatter into a ring.
Deimos, smaller and farther, drifts outward to safety.
Share this: tell someone Mars has two moons tonight and price their surprise.

items.title: The Tallest Range
items.question: Mount Everest sits in which mountain range?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the Himalayas: the planet's highest range, still growing a few millimetres a year.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the Himalayas. India is still ramming into Asia, and the collision keeps lifting the range — Everest grows taller while you read this. Fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres all stand in these mountains.
items.lessonContent:
The Himalayas are a slow-motion collision: India driving into Asia, lifting rock skyward.
Everest grows a few millimetres yearly — the range is unfinished business.
Fourteen eight-thousanders stand in these mountains and nowhere else.
The same collision fuels the region's great earthquakes.
Share this: explain tonight why the world's tallest mountains are still under construction.

items.title: The Water Formula
items.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
items.correctExplanation: Right — H2O: two hydrogens bonded to one oxygen.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: H2O. Two hydrogen atoms share electrons with one oxygen in a bent arrangement — and that bend gives water nearly all its strange talents, from surface tension to dissolving power. Three letters, one planet's whole chemistry set.
items.lessonContent:
H2O's bent shape makes it polar — one end faintly positive, the other faintly negative.
That polarity dissolves salts, builds surface tension, and floats ice.
Water's strangeness is chemistry's most consequential accident.
Life may depend on no other molecule so completely.
Share this: draw the Mickey-Mouse head of H2O tonight — ears of hydrogen, face of oxygen.

items.title: Boiling Point
items.question: At sea level, water boils at how many degrees Celsius?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — 100 degrees Celsius: the scale's upper anchor, defined at sea-level pressure.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 100. Celsius pinned its boiling point to water at sea level — zero at freezing, one hundred at boiling. Climb a mountain and the number drops, because thinner air lets bubbles form with less heat.
items.lessonContent:
Celsius anchors 0 to freezing and 100 to boiling — at sea level, always add the pressure.
Higher altitudes boil cooler: climbers brew weak tea for physics reasons.
Pressure cookers reverse the trick, boiling hotter than 100.
Kelvin keeps the same degree size and simply starts at absolute zero.
Share this: guess your kettle's whistle temperature before checking — then climb to change it.

items.title: The Hottest World
items.question: Which planet has the hottest surface, even though it is not the closest to the Sun?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Venus: a runaway greenhouse effect bakes it hotter than Mercury ever gets.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Venus. Its crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat so completely that the surface melts lead — around 465 degrees. Proximity loses to atmosphere: Mercury, nearer the Sun, stays cooler for lack of a blanket.
items.lessonContent:
Venus is the cautionary tale of runaway greenhouse warming — heat in, almost none out.
Its surface could melt lead, though it orbits farther than Mercury.
Soviet landers survived there for about an hour each — heroic engineering against hell.
Understanding Venus is partly how we model Earth's own climate levers.
Share this: tell someone the hottest planet isn't the nearest, and watch the blanket explanation land.
